case_name: CASE OF MLADINA D.D. LJUBLJANA v. SLOVENIA (No. 2)

assessment.Existence of an interference: The applicant company, as the publisher of Mladina magazine, was subjected to an interference with its freedom of expression. The domestic courts ordered it to publish an apology in Mladina (see paragraph 17) and to pay compensation to B.G. (see paragraphs 25-30), which constitutes a clear interference with its right under Article 10 of the Convention (see paragraph 13 for the initial claim and paragraphs 15-30 for the subsequent judicial decisions). Thus, there has been an interference with the applicant’s freedom of expression, and we proceed to the next step.
assessment.Lawfulness of the interference: The interference was based on domestic law. The civil claims brought by B.G. relied on Articles 178 and 179 of the Code of Obligations (see paragraph 33) and the relevant constitutional provisions (see paragraphs 32-35). The domestic courts explicitly applied these legal provisions in their rulings (see paragraphs 15, 18, 20, 22-24). Therefore, the interference had a basis in Slovenian domestic law, and we proceed to the next step.
assessment.Legitimate aims of the interference: The interference pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation and rights of others, as defined in Article 10(2) of the Convention. B.G. initiated the defamation proceedings to protect his honour, good name, and dignity, as well as those of his family (see paragraph 13). The domestic courts, including the Constitutional Court, explicitly balanced the applicant’s right to freedom of expression against B.G.’s personality rights (see paragraphs 15, 18, 20, 24). Thus, the interference was aimed at protecting a legitimate interest under Article 10(2), and we proceed to the final step.
assessment.Necessary in a democratic society: To assess whether the interference was necessary in a democratic society, the following must be considered: (a) whether there was a pressing social need for the interference; (b) whether the measure employed was the least restrictive possible; and (c) whether the domestic authorities provided relevant and sufficient reasons for the interference. (a) There was a public interest in the debate surrounding the comparison between B.G. and Joseph Goebbels (see paragraph 6), but the domestic courts found that the publication of the family photographs in the satirical section transcended this debate by creating a visual and direct comparison between B.G.’s family and Goebbels’ family, rather than focusing on political methods (see paragraphs 18, 20, 24). (b) The domestic courts ordered a civil remedy—an apology and monetary compensation (see paragraphs 17, 25-30)—which is less restrictive than criminal penalties or prior restraint, thus satisfying the least restrictive means requirement. (c) The domestic courts, particularly the Constitutional Court, provided thorough reasoning for their decisions. They distinguished between the text, which critique d political methods, and the photographs, which they deemed to create an unacceptable comparison between the families (see paragraph 24). The Constitutional Court emphasized that the inclusion of B.G.’s children, who are private individuals, tipped the balance in favour of protecting their rights (see paragraph 24). Additionally, the Court noted that even though B.G. was a public figure and had exposed his family to public attention, this did not equate to consent for the photographs to be used in such a highly offensive and non-consensual context (see paragraphs 10, 15, 24). The ECtHR has previously ruled that freedom of expression, while fundamental, does not extend to gratuitously offensive content that does not contribute to public debate, especially when it involves private individuals such as children (see no. 44179/98 and no. 60641/08). Furthermore, the Court has held that photographs can have a more profound impact than text alone, warranting stricter scrutiny (see no. 59320/00 and no. 40660/08). The domestic courts’ reasoning aligns with these principles, as they carefully weighed the competing interests and concluded that the visual comparison in this specific context was not protected. Consequently, the interference can be regarded as necessary in a democratic society.
